title: Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol for IPv6 (DHCPv6)
summary: This standards-track document describes DHCPv6, an extensible mechanism for configuring nodes with network parameters, IP addresses and prefixes. Parameters can be given statelessly or together with stateful assignment of addresses or prefixes. It was later replaced by RFC 9915.

plainLanguage.summary: A new computer asks a helper for an address and settings so it can join the network. It was later replaced by RFC 9915.

questions: how do hosts get ipv6 addresses from a server
how does dhcpv6 prefix delegation work
what is a duid in dhcpv6
subtitle: How IPv6 hosts and routers ask a server for addresses, delegated prefixes and network settings.

tldr.problem: IPv6 devices often need more than stateless autoconfiguration can give them: addresses handed out under network policy, whole prefixes for routers behind them, and settings such as DNS and NTP servers.
tldr.mechanism: DHCPv6 is a client/server protocol over UDP. A client finds servers with a multicast Solicit, receives addresses, prefixes and options grouped into Identity Associations, and keeps them alive with Renew and Rebind. Relay agents carry messages to servers on other links.
tldr.outcome: RFC 8415 merges the original DHCPv6 specification with prefix delegation, stateless DHCPv6 and several fixes into one document, and it has itself since been obsoleted by RFC 9915.

today: RFC 8415 is a Proposed Standard that has itself been obsoleted by RFC 9915, so new work should follow the newer document. It replaced RFC 3315, RFC 3633, RFC 3736, RFC 4242, RFC 7083, RFC 7283 and RFC 7550.

sections.title: What DHCPv6 Provides
sections.content:
RFC 8415 describes DHCPv6, a client/server protocol that provides managed configuration of devices. In its basic form it configures clients on the same link as the server. A relay agent function lets clients and servers on different links talk to each other.

A server can give a client addresses and other configuration data, which travels in options. New options can be defined later, so the protocol is extensible. DHCPv6 can also delegate whole IPv6 prefixes to a requesting router, and it can serve just the other settings with no addresses at all. That last mode is called stateless DHCPv6, because the server keeps no state for the client.

This document is a consolidation. It folds in the original DHCPv6 specification (RFC 3315), prefix delegation (RFC 3633), stateless DHCPv6 (RFC 3736), the refresh-time option (RFC 4242), client throttling (RFC 7083), relay handling of unknown messages (RFC 7283) and clarifications on mixing models (RFC 7550), and it obsoletes all of them. It also covers errata filed against the older RFCs.

For IPv4 configuration the IETF consensus is that DHCPv4 should be used rather than DHCPv6. For IPv6-only networks, RFC 7341 describes a transport that carries DHCPv4 messages over DHCPv6.
sections.plainLanguage: DHCPv6 is the way a device asks a helper for an address and for settings like where to find the phone book (DNS). If the helper is on another street, a messenger (a relay) carries the question over.

sections.title: Operational Models
sections.content:
The RFC describes several common ways to use DHCPv6. They are not mutually exclusive: a device may get an address statefully and later ask for extra parameters statelessly.

  • Stateless DHCP: the client wants only other configuration, such as DNS servers or search lists. It needs just two messages, Information-request and Reply.
  • Non-temporary addresses: the original motivation for DHCP. It suits cases where stateless address autoconfiguration alone is insufficient or impractical, for example because of network policy or dynamic DNS updates. Each address has a preferred and a valid lifetime, and the client must stop using it when the valid lifetime ends.
  • Temporary addresses: added to give privacy support when stateful assignment is used. A client is NOT RECOMMENDED to renew them.
  • Prefix delegation: a server (the delegating router) hands a prefix to a client (the requesting router), for example an ISP giving a subscriber's router a prefix that it then subnets. In the example, a delegated /48 is split into /64 prefixes, one per link.
  • Customer edge routers: combine address assignment and prefix delegation in a single set of transactions.

A client can hold several addresses by sending several IA_NA options. For prefixes, a typical operator prefers to delegate one larger prefix, so clients are advised to ask for a larger prefix up front rather than request more later. Whether to grant extras is server policy.

If a client builds addresses from a delegated prefix, those addresses' lifetimes MUST NOT exceed the remaining lifetimes of the delegated prefix. The same holds for any prefix advertised for SLAAC.
sections.plainLanguage: Sometimes you only want directions (settings). Sometimes you want a house number (an address). Sometimes a whole street of numbers to give out to your own neighbors (a prefix). DHCPv6 can do any of these, or all together.

sections.title: Message Formats
sections.content:
All messages between clients and servers share one fixed header followed by a variable-length options area. The header is a 1-octet msg-type and a 3-octet transaction-id. All values are in network byte order, options are packed with no padding, and messages ride in UDP: clients listen on port 546, while servers and relay agents listen on port 547.

Thirteen message types are defined. A client uses Solicit to find servers, Request to get leases from a chosen server, Confirm to check that its addresses still fit the link, Renew and Rebind to extend lifetimes, Release and Decline to give leases back, and Information-request to get settings without leases. A server answers with Advertise or Reply, and may send Reconfigure to prompt a client to update.

Relay agents use two more messages, Relay-forward and Relay-reply, which share one format: msg-type, hop-count, a 16-octet link-address that helps the server identify the client's link, a 16-octet peer-address holding the address the relayed message came from, and options that MUST include a Relay Message option carrying the original message. In a Relay-reply the hop count, link address and peer address are copied from the Relay-forward.

Clients send to the link-scoped multicast address ff02::1:2 (All_DHCP_Relay_Agents_and_Servers), so no server address needs to be configured. Relays can use the site-scoped ff05::1:3 (All_DHCP_Servers). Domain names in options are encoded as in RFC 1035 and MUST NOT be compressed.
sections.plainLanguage: Every DHCPv6 note starts with a tiny label saying what kind of note it is and a random number to match replies. After that comes a list of extra items. Messengers wrap the original note inside a bigger envelope.

sections.title: DUIDs and Identity Associations
sections.content:
Every client and server has exactly one DUID, a DHCP Unique Identifier. Servers use it to recognise clients, and clients use it to name a particular server. A DUID is a 2-octet type code followed by an identifier of at least 1 and at most 128 octets. Clients and servers MUST treat DUIDs as opaque and only compare them for equality. A DUID SHOULD NOT change over time if at all possible.

Four types are defined: link-layer address plus time (1), vendor-assigned unique ID based on Enterprise Number (2), link-layer address (3) and UUID (4). Having several types exists because the identifier must be globally unique but easy to generate on very different devices, some of which have no persistent storage. A DUID-LLT MUST be kept in stable storage, and devices without stable storage MUST NOT use it.

An Identity Association (IA) groups related leases for a client. Each has a client-chosen IAID, which MUST be unique among that client's IAs of the same type and stay consistent across restarts. Three IA types exist: IA_NA for non-temporary addresses, IA_TA for temporary addresses and IA_PD for delegated prefixes. An address IA belongs to exactly one interface, whereas an IA_PD may be tied to the client, a set of interfaces or one interface. A server's binding for an IA is indexed by DUID, IA type and IAID.
sections.plainLanguage: A DUID is your name tag, and it never changes. An IA is a labelled box where your borrowed addresses go, and the label (the IAID) has to be the same every time you come back.

sections.title: The Configuration Exchanges
sections.content:
To get leases, a client creates its IAs and multicasts a Solicit. This is server discovery. Servers that can help answer with Advertise. The client collects advertisements for the first retransmission period, unless one arrives with a preference value of 255, which it takes at once. It then sends a Request naming the chosen server by DUID, and that server commits the leases and answers with a Reply.

A client can ask for a faster two-message exchange by adding the Rapid Commit option to its Solicit. A willing server commits the leases first and replies directly. The RFC warns that if more than one server answers, all but one will hold leases the client does not use, so this suits setups where only one server responds.

Each lease has T1 and T2 times. At T1 the client sends Renew to the original server. If that fails, at T2 it sends Rebind to any server. If every valid lifetime runs out, it starts again with Solicit. The recommended T1 and T2 are 0.5 and 0.8 of the shortest preferred lifetime, and a value of 0 means the client chooses its own times. A server MUST return the same T1 and T2 for all IAs in a Reply so the client can renew everything in one go.

When finished, the client sends Release, after it has stopped using the leases. After the client performs duplicate address detection on a new address and finds it already in use, it sends Decline. After a possible move to a new link, a client with only addresses sends Confirm, whereas one with delegated prefixes sends Rebind. A client that needs only settings sends Information-request, and the Information Refresh Time option says when to ask again.

A server may send Reconfigure to tell a client to start a Renew, Rebind or Information-request. The client should be suspicious of it, because Reconfigure messages may be faked. Once a client has a Server Unicast option from a server, it SHOULD unicast Request, Renew, Release and Decline to that server.

Servers MUST discard Solicit, Confirm, Rebind and Information-request messages that arrive with a unicast destination address. Messages with an unknown message type MUST be discarded, but unknown options MUST be ignored rather than causing a discard, which is critical for future extensions.
sections.plainLanguage: You shout 'anyone have an address for me?', helpers say 'I do!', you pick one, and it gives you an address for a while. Before the time is up you ask to keep it. When you leave, you hand it back politely.

sections.title: Retransmission and Rate Limiting
sections.content:
Clients are responsible for reliable delivery of their own messages, since UDP does not provide it. If no reply comes, the client retransmits with exponential backoff. Each timeout RT is doubled from the previous one, with a randomization factor RAND between -0.1 and +0.1 to keep many clients from synchronizing. The backoff is capped by a per-message maximum time (MRT), and optionally by a maximum retry count (MRC) or maximum duration (MRD). The client MUST update the Elapsed Time option in each retransmission and MUST keep the same transaction ID.

Each message type has its own parameters. For example, Solicit starts at 1 second and is capped at 3600 seconds, while Request starts at 1 second, is capped at 30 seconds and gives up after 10 attempts. The first Solicit SHOULD be delayed by a random time up to 1 second, which desynchronizes clients after something like a power failure.

To prevent loops, a client MUST limit the rate of messages it sends, per interface. A token bucket is suggested, with a possible default of 20 packets in 20 seconds. If a server sets T1 or T2 to 0, the client MUST pick its own time and MUST NOT transmit immediately.
sections.plainLanguage: If nobody answers your knock, you wait a bit and knock again, waiting longer each time and a little randomly so a whole crowd of people does not knock at the exact same moment. And you never knock a hundred times a second.

sections.title: Relay Agents
sections.content:
A relay agent on the client's link wraps client messages so that servers elsewhere can answer, and the client does not notice. By default, a relay that has not been explicitly configured MUST use the All_DHCP_Servers multicast address, though it SHOULD be configured with a list of destinations that includes unicast addresses.

When a relay receives a client message, it builds a Relay-forward. It copies the sender's address into peer-address, puts the original message into a Relay Message option, and sets hop-count to 0. It fills link-address with a global or unique-local address from the client's link, so the server can pick suitable addresses. If it cannot identify the return interface from that address, it MUST add an Interface-Id option, which the server echoes back.

Relays can be chained. A relay receiving a Relay-forward increments the hop count, and discards the message if the count has already reached the HOP_COUNT_LIMIT of 8. A relay that does not recognise a message type MUST still forward it. Prefix delegation is relayed the same way as addresses, but the server may need out-of-band means to set up routes for delegated prefixes.
sections.plainLanguage: A relay is a mail carrier between streets. It puts your letter in a bigger envelope that says which street it came from, and when the answer comes back it unwraps the envelope and hands it to you.

sections.title: Options and Status Codes
sections.content:
Every option has a 2-octet code, a 2-octet length and its data. Options can be nested: an IA_NA (code 3) carries IA Address options inside it, and an IA_PD (code 25) carries IA Prefix options (code 26). Most options are singletons that may appear only once. The exceptions are IA_NA, IA_TA, Vendor Class, Vendor-specific Information and IA_PD.

The base set covers identity (Client Identifier, Server Identifier), leases (IA_NA, IA_TA, IA_PD and their address and prefix options), negotiation (Option Request, Preference, Rapid Commit, Reconfigure Accept, Server Unicast), plumbing (Elapsed Time, Relay Message, Interface-Id, Authentication, Reconfigure Message), vendor data (User Class, Vendor Class, Vendor-specific Information) and timing (Information Refresh Time, SOL_MAX_RT, INF_MAX_RT). The last two let a server tune a client's maximum retransmission timeouts.

Results are carried in the Status Code option, which can appear at the message level or inside an IA. If no Status Code option is present, the status is assumed to be Success. A server answers NotOnLink if an address prefix does not fit the client's link, NoAddrsAvail or NoPrefixAvail when it has nothing to give, and UseMulticast to force a client back to multicast.
sections.plainLanguage: Options are the little labelled slips of paper stuffed in each envelope: 'here is your address', 'here is the phone book', 'sorry, none left'. Every slip says what it is and how long it is.

sections.title: Authentication and Security
sections.content:
The RFC says the threat to DHCP is inherently an insider threat, and that DHCP lacks end-to-end encryption between clients and servers, so hijacking, tampering and eavesdropping are possible. A rogue server can feed a client bad configuration, for example to set up a man-in-the-middle for DNS or NTP, or to break its connectivity.

Two mechanisms are defined. Messages between servers and relay agents can be authenticated and encrypted with IPsec, as described in RFC 8213. For clients, the Reconfiguration Key Authentication Protocol (RKAP) guards against forged Reconfigure messages. The server sends a 128-bit reconfigure key in the initial Reply, and later Reconfigure messages carry an HMAC-MD5 computed with that key. A client MUST discard any Reconfigure message that lacks valid authentication. The RFC admits RKAP can be compromised by an attacker who intercepts the key sent in plain text.

Other advice includes using unpredictable transaction IDs, rate-limiting, and limiting the number of leases per client to blunt resource-exhaustion attacks. Servers SHOULD NOT generate predictable addresses by default. For privacy, the RFC points to RFC 7824 and RFC 7844.
sections.plainLanguage: Anybody can shout 'I am the address helper!' on a network. RKAP is a secret handshake: the real helper tells you a secret word the first time, and later orders to change things only count if they include that word.

sections.title: Obsoleted Mechanisms
sections.content:
A few mechanisms from the original DHCPv6 were dropped because they were not widely deployed, were underspecified or had operational problems. Legacy implementations MAY support them, but conformant ones MUST NOT rely on them.

  • Delayed authentication was underspecified and an operational burden, with extremely limited adoption after 10 years.
  • Lifetime hints from clients caused trouble because some clients sent remaining lifetimes instead of total desired ones, which servers could read as a request for ever-shrinking leases. Clients now SHOULD set them to 0, and servers MUST ignore them.
  • T1/T2 hints from clients had similar issues. Clients SHOULD send 0, and servers MUST ignore client-supplied values.
sections.plainLanguage: A few old rules did not work well in practice, so the new rulebook says 'don't use these any more'.

messages.label: Solicit
messages.note: Multicast, so every server on the link hears it.

messages.label: Advertise
messages.note: Client collects Advertises and selects a configuration.

messages.label: Renew
messages.note: Sent when the T1 timer expires.

fields.name: transaction-id
fields.desc: Matches responses to the exchange, a 3-octet field. Options follow, filling the rest of the message.

fields.name: hop-count
fields.desc: Number of relay agents that have already relayed this message.

fields.name: link-address
fields.desc: Address the server can use to identify the client's link.

fields.name: peer-address
fields.desc: Address of the client or relay the message was received from.

items.label: SOLICIT
items.desc: Client locates servers.

items.label: ADVERTISE
items.desc: Server announces it is available.

items.label: REQUEST
items.desc: Client requests configuration from a specific server.

items.label: CONFIRM
items.desc: Client checks that its addresses are still appropriate to the link.

items.label: RENEW
items.desc: Client asks the original server to extend lease lifetimes.

items.label: REBIND
items.desc: Client asks any server to extend lifetimes after Renew gets no response.

items.label: REPLY
items.desc: Server returns leases, parameters or an acknowledgement.

items.label: RELEASE
items.desc: Client gives up leases.

items.label: DECLINE
items.desc: Client reports addresses already in use on the link.

items.label: RECONFIGURE
items.desc: Server tells client to fetch updated configuration.

items.label: INFORMATION-REQUEST
items.desc: Client asks for parameters without leases.

items.label: RELAY-FORW
items.desc: Relay agent forwards a message toward servers.

items.label: RELAY-REPL
items.desc: Server sends a message back through relays.

cells: Vendor-assigned unique ID based on Enterprise Number

data.title: Computing RT
data.code:
RT = IRT + RAND*IRT              (first transmission)
RT = 2*RTprev + RAND*RTprev      (each later transmission)

if (RT > MRT)
   RT = MRT + RAND*MRT

items.label: Success
items.desc: Success.

items.label: UnspecFail
items.desc: Failure, reason unspecified.

items.label: NoAddrsAvail
items.desc: The server has no addresses available to assign to the IA(s).

items.label: NoBinding
items.desc: Client record (binding) unavailable.

items.label: NotOnLink
items.desc: The prefix for the address is not appropriate for the client's link.

items.label: UseMulticast
items.desc: Forces the client to send messages using the All_DHCP_Relay_Agents_and_Servers multicast address.

items.label: NoPrefixAvail
items.desc: The server has no prefixes available to assign to the IA_PD(s).
